newsitem.title: UK: Britain frosty on Sinn Fein truce comments.
newsitem.headline: Britain frosty on Sinn Fein truce comments.

text.p: Britain dampened hopes of movement in Northern Ireland's crippled peace process on Monday, saying the IRA's Sinn Fein political arm had not yet met its terms for a seat in talks.

Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew gave a frosty response to weekend comments by Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams who said he would push for a guerrilla truce if Britain made concessions to bring his party into peace negotiations.
"It was all too familiar and, therefore, insufficient," Mayhew told reporters.

In a wide-ranging newspaper article Adams said that "if clear assurances are given by the British government that a negotiations process which is both viable and credible will be put in place, then the peace process can be restored."

The Dublin-published Irish Times, which carried the article, said Adams might have been giving a coded-signal to Britain that Sinn Fein and the Irish Republican Army wanted to bridge a gulf that has blighted peace efforts for more than year.
"Everybody wants to see all elected parties at the table," Mayhew said.
"They have to be there on the same basis as each other, that is to say (on the basis of) a declared and abundantly clear commitment to exclusively peaceful and democratic methods."

Mayhew spoke within hours of the funeral in England of Stephen Restorick, the second soldier to be killed since last October when the IRA stepped up hostilities in Northern Ireland after a bombing campaign concentrated on mainland Britain.
The IRA has not admitted the attack but British security forces are convinced it was the work of guerrillas who want Northern Ireland merged into an all-Ireland state.
The killing, by sniper fire on February 12 at a border vehicle checkpoint, caused outrage in Britain and Ireland.

Britain says the IRA must abandon a 28-year war against London's sovereignty over Northern Ireland before Sinn Fein will be given a seat in all party talks. Its intelligence services will assess whether any future IRA truce is intended to be permanent.
Republicans say the IRA will not halt hostilities until Britain signals speedy entry for Sinn Fein into the talks.
Sinn Fein says that as a legitimate political party with 15.5 per cent of the vote it has a right to be included unconditionally.

British leaders argue that a 17-month ceasefire that ended last year was never meant to last and was used by the extremists to fuel the restart of a bombing and shooting campaign that has escalated this year in Northern Ireland.
So far the conflict has claimed more than 3,200 civilian, security force and guerrilla victims.
